projects.title: Starship Booster Cryo Proof Tooling
projects.summary: As Responsible Engineer for Super Heavy’s cryo-proof tooling, I carried the program from redesign and structural validation through procurement, assembly, and vehicle integration, with a focus on reliable testing and faster production.

points.text: The 13,000+ component assembly sealed the booster’s 33 engine feedlines during cryo-proof testing. I redesigned the tooling to accommodate a high-flow gaseous-oxygen test assembly, a drain manifold for post-test cryogenic fluid removal, and gas-system ports for decay checks and transducer testing with the Checkouts team.

The inherited assembly had unnecessary leak paths, a complicated bolted stackup, and no reliable CAD reference. I rebuilt the assembly model and replaced the plate-to-drain bolted stackup with a custom welded elbow that located its own orientation for welding. I also coordinated plate-interface changes with the propulsion responsible engineer and replaced specialized bolts with standard factory hardware.

I ran FEA on maximum-pressure feedline blow-off load cases to check the tooling under cryo-proof loading. These pressure-induced separation loads guided the structural checks at the interfaces that retained the tooling on the vehicle.

I directed $800,000 in machined-part procurement, working through daily vendor calls to keep delivery on schedule and parts conforming to the drawings. Daily stand-ups and status updates to more than 80 stakeholders kept design, supply, build, and integration teams aligned.

I oversaw up to 25 technicians during subassembly build and vehicle integration, resolving issues on the floor as they arose. I also physically installed tooling on the vehicle to work through fit issues firsthand and designed lineside parts storage to support the build sequence.

Across the program, design improvements, streamlined planning, and better parts storage saved more than 1,100 production hours per vehicle. The work extended from how the tooling performed during a test to how efficiently the team could prepare, assemble, and integrate it.

projects.note: Design work performed at SpaceX is proprietary. No CAD, drawings, part numbers, or hardware imagery are shown.

projects.title: Starship Production Tooling
projects.summary: On SpaceX’s Structures Build Engineering team, I helped design and build a new weld-focused subassembly cell for a high-pressure propulsion manifold for Starship V3. My work included flange fit-up fixtures, lift and access tooling, flight-part retrofits, and production improvements.

points.text: I helped develop the manifold build cell and oversaw its integration on the production floor. I managed approximately $50,000 in purchased parts to equip the cell and support the build process.

I designed self-clocking fixtures to position and orient the manifold’s endpoint flanges for weld fit-up. This work taught me to apply geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) to the tooling interfaces that controlled flange alignment.
I designed a lift tool rated for a 1,100 lb working load limit. The tool was proof-tested at twice that limit, or 2,200 lb, to validate it before use.
I designed a tool that improved technician access and the integration process for Starship’s aft flap torque frames.

I designed five flight-part retrofits to accommodate off-nominal conditions in existing assemblies. I took precise measurements of the as-built hardware, created CAD models of those assemblies, and used them to define custom parts for manufacture and installation.
Alongside the build cell and integration tooling, I designed several 3D-printed parts and parts manufactured through Protolabs to improve production rate.

projects.headline: Starship Production Tooling
projects.unit: labor hours saved per vehicle with access tooling
projects.challenge: Hold tube and flange alignment across a nine-meter weld cell, then safely move and integrate the assembly.
projects.decision: Design the weld fixtures and handling tools together. Use as-built CAD when flight hardware needed a retrofit.
projects.proof: A 1,100 lb lift tool, proof-tested at 2× working load. Five owned flight-part retrofits. An access tool that saved 50 labor hours per vehicle.
projects.takeaway: A fixture has to locate the part accurately and give the person building it room to work.

projects.title: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.summary: I designed the rotor and mount for reliable braking within the drivetrain package, combining material tradeoffs, thermal analysis, structural FEA, and temperature testing.

points.text: I coordinated space claims with the powertrain team so the rotor would fit the drivetrain assembly. Long-term reliability was the main goal, with a design requirement to tolerate temperatures up to 500°C with a safety margin.

I compared cast iron and 4140 steel in a material decision matrix. The study weighed cast iron’s density and thermal-conductivity advantages against fatigue performance, and I selected steel for its endurance-limit advantage in that comparison.

I chose titanium buttons for their low thermal conductivity, strength-to-weight ratio, and corrosion resistance. They act as a thermal choke between the steel disc and the lightweight 7075 aluminum mount, which interfaces with the differential bolts.

I first sized rotor thickness using a conservative case in which maximum braking energy became heat with no heat escaping. I then refined the sizing through transient heat-transfer analysis, considering conduction, forced convection, and radiation.

I used curved face slots for pad debris removal, de-gassing, and water clearance, accepting additional pad wear. In Ansys, I fixed the pad contact regions and distributed the maximum rules-based braking moment through the mount’s bolted connections to check stress states.
I tested the rotors with temperature crayons to assess their operating temperatures. Manufacturing was outsourced for three-axis CNC machining.

projects.decision: Compare cast iron with 4140 steel, use titanium buttons to limit heat flow into an aluminum mount, and refine rotor thickness through transient thermal analysis.
projects.proof: Checked the rotor in Ansys with supports at the pad contact regions and braking moment applied through the mount bolt locations. Used temperature crayons to assess operating temperatures and outsourced manufacturing to a three-axis CNC supplier.
projects.takeaway: Long-term reliability guided the material choices, thermal sizing, and structural checks.

caliperSelection.rationale: Sponsorship availability was the deciding factor. The Brembo had the largest listed pad area, tied the ISR for the largest listed piston area, and weighed less than the ISR. The AP Racing option was lighter and the Wilwood was less expensive; the comparison did not identify a clear winner across all criteria.

projects.title: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.summary: I designed a rear hub and bearing assembly that brought the drivetrain, wheel, and electronics interfaces together in a lightweight, manufacturable package.

points.text: I collaborated with the drivetrain and electronics teams to define the assembly’s interfaces. The hub needed to accommodate the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and integrate the electronics team’s Hall effect sensors.

I evaluated bearings in SKF SimPro Quick within an 80–85 mm inner-diameter and 110–120 mm outer-diameter envelope. The selection informed hub thickness and packaging. I compared titanium, 6061, and 7075 aluminum, selecting 7075-T6.

I applied wheel loads from the team’s truss solver to the wheel flange, modeled the tensile load from the center-lock nut, and included bearing forces and drivetrain torque at the tripod interface. I sized hub-nut engagement using bolt tensile and nut thread-shear areas.
I started with geometry that satisfied the system interfaces and bearing constraints, then removed excess material through pocketing and checked the revised hub in Ansys.
The rotational features were turned on a lathe first. CNC milling then produced the tripod cutout, dowel-pin holes, brake-button holes, and wheel-flange pockets.

projects.headline: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.challenge: Define a rear hub assembly around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall effect sensors, while meeting structural and manufacturing requirements.
projects.decision: Use the system interfaces and bearing selection to establish the hub geometry and thickness, compare titanium with 6061 and 7075 aluminum, then size the threaded hub nut connection and optimize pocketing with FEA.
projects.proof: Checked cornering and braking loads, bearing performance in SKF SimPro Quick, and hub behavior in Ansys. Manufacturing included lathe operations on several features and tooling the part for a three-axis CNC mill.
projects.takeaway: The drivetrain and electronics interfaces set the requirements. Bearing selection, structural analysis, and machining constraints then shaped the hub.
projects.discipline: System integration / Bearing selection / Mechanical design

bearingSelection.method: Build the assembly in SKF SimPro Quick and sweep the candidate bearings. Work with Powertrain to set the allowable inner diameter.
bearingSelection.validation: Selected the SKF 71817 ACDGB/VQ253 angular-contact bearing after reviewing fatigue life, load capacity, and power loss across wheel speeds.

projects.title: Carbon Pushrod & Swept Control Arms
projects.summary: I developed and fabricated a lighter suspension assembly, pairing carbon-fiber pushrods with steel control arms and checking both the bonded joints and on-car clearance.

points.text: The control arms had to connect the upright, chassis tabs, and pushrods. I kept steel for the control arms, where the team had greater confidence in the manufacturing process, and used carbon fiber for the pushrods to reduce mass.

I tested the carbon-fiber pushrods in tension and compression on an Instron. For fabrication, I cut the tubes to length and turned aluminum end plugs, controlling the bonding-surface diameter to within half a thousandth of an inch.

I replaced a heavy mounting plate with gussets at the apex. I cut steel tubing, turned and milled end plugs, bored and reamed bearing seats in laser-cut plates, and welded and tapped the plugs for rod ends.

During freshman-year integration, a missed tolerance stackup caused the apex to interfere at maximum steer. We checked the required material removal in Ansys and ground the existing apex to recover clearance. The combined suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb.

gallery.cap: Upper apex von Mises: 38.6 ksi max

projects.headline: Pushrods & Control Arms
projects.unit: less suspension mass than the prior design
projects.challenge: At integration, the control-arm apex interfered before the car reached maximum steer. A tolerance stackup we had missed in the design caused the clearance problem.
projects.decision: Model the exact material removal needed at the apex, check the revised geometry in Ansys, then use an angle grinder to remove that material from the existing part.
projects.proof: The revised apex made maximum steer possible. The original suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb through the apex-mounted gussets and carbon-fiber pushrods.
projects.takeaway: That experience taught me how much engineering is working through the problem in front of you, one constraint at a time.

projects.title: Discrete Ride Height Adjustment
projects.summary: I designed a shim-based attachment to make ride-height changes more repeatable, replacing a process that relied on turning an opposite-thread pushrod.

points.text: The mechanism changes pushrod length by adding or removing shims and retightening the fasteners. The attachment connects to the inboard suspension mechanism and keeps the shim stack in compression.
I designed the attachment in 7075 aluminum and kept the shim pockets concentric with the retaining bolts. Lightweight shim geometry reduced the mass added by the adjustment mechanism.
I checked the attachment under pushrod loading in SolidWorks FEA. The shims were laser-cut and the attachment pieces machined. The upper component’s CNC machining was handled by another team member.
The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car in exchange for a more repeatable setup adjustment.

projects.proof: SolidWorks FEA checked the attachment under pushrod loading. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car.
projects.takeaway: A small weight penalty bought a more repeatable adjustment for the team at the track.

projects.title: Motion-Capture Integration for Swarm Manufacturing
projects.summary: I developed software that gave robots real-time position data for swarm-manufacturing research at UT Austin’s SiDi Lab.

points.text: The lab needed its robots to know their position during coordinated manufacturing tasks.
I connected the infrared motion-capture system to a robotic arm and its driver software using Python and the NatNet SDK.
The integration made real-time tracking data available to the robot software. I presented the work to UT research faculty.

projects.headline: Robotics Motion Capture
projects.challenge: Make motion-capture position data available to a robotic system used in swarm-manufacturing research.
projects.decision: Integrate the camera system with the arm’s driver software through Python and the NatNet SDK.
projects.proof: Enabled real-time position tracking and presented the work to UT research faculty.
projects.takeaway: The useful result was a working connection between the sensor data and the robot software.

projects.title: Adjustable Hose-Carrying Assembly
projects.summary: I designed a linked carrier to guide hydraulic hoses through a drill rig’s motion while keeping the routing clear of surrounding hardware.

points.text: The hoses needed to move between their stored and operating positions without interference.
I gave each carrier link rotational freedom, fixed one end, and constrained the other to a sketched path in SolidWorks.
The routing could be revised through the sketch while preserving the linked assembly’s motion.

projects.headline: Hydraulic Hose Carrier
projects.challenge: Guide hydraulic hoses through the rig’s motion without interference.
projects.decision: Give each link rotational freedom, fix one end of the carrier, and let the other follow a sketched path in SolidWorks.
projects.proof: A path-mated assembly with an interference-conscious route and a linkage designed for the required motion.
projects.takeaway: The route lives in a sketch, so the assembly can follow a revised path without re-mating each link.
